turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Monday, October 5th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Brazil first, because the polls were wrong in a way that matters. Yesterday's first round ended with Flávio Bolsonaro at roughly 47% and President Lula at roughly 45%, with more than 99% of the vote counted, and polls just days earlier had Lula comfortably ahead.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The runoff is October 25th, so we get 3 weeks of a campaign that is now Lula's to lose. Flávio is 45, the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, and he ran on crime, corruption and a barely concealed alignment with Washington. Lula's own line afterwards was that he had been convinced he would win outright in the first round, which tells you how much the internal numbers lied to him too.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The polling miss is the story inside the story. Bloomberg's framing was that Bolsonaro pushed Lula to the brink of defeat, and the pattern is familiar: the right outperforming the final surveys in a country where phone and online panels under-sample exactly the voters who are fed up. For the world's 8th largest economy, the market question is fiscal. A Bolsonaro win would be read as a break from Lula's spending path, and a first-round lead in the congressional races matters as much as the presidency.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Staying with war and politics, Yemen. On Sunday the chairman of the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced a full-scale military campaign to retake all Houthi-held territory, Sanaa included. This is the government side going on offense, not a Houthi strike. The government claims 257 precision targeting operations and an initial toll of at least 700 Houthi fighters killed, and that figure is the government's own claim, not independently confirmed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The timing is the tell. This is a week when Hormuz and oil are already stressed, and Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon were reported again on Sunday. A Yemen offensive reopens the Red Sea question just as the G7 and the IEA are trying to cool energy markets. If the Houthis answer by widening attacks on shipping, the diesel reserve release we saw last week starts to look small.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And a dangerous border incident in South Asia. On Friday in the Ferozepur sector of Indian Punjab, Indian border guards shot and killed 2 Pakistani civilians. On Saturday both capitals summoned each other's senior diplomat. India says 3 people ignored warnings and moved toward the fence, and calls Pakistan's account baseless and motivated. Pakistan says they were unarmed civilians and the shooting was unprovoked.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The number of the week is 29,000. That is September payrolls against a consensus of about 85,000, and the revisions took another 60,000 jobs away: August cut to 133,000 from 162,000, and July now shows a loss of 10,000. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, though much of that is people entering the labor force rather than layoffs, and average hourly earnings rose just 5 cents, or 0.1%, to $37.81.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What makes it awkward is that the Fed was debating a hike, not a cut. With energy prices surging and inflation running hot, the committee is staring at stagflation. Markets now price about 84% odds of a hold in October, and the September minutes land on Wednesday, so that is the next place to look for how many officials were actually leaning toward tightening.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second-order read is that bad-news-is-good-news has limits. Equities rallied on the print, but the 10-year yield went from 5.18% intraday back to around 5.28% by the close, because a weak labor market does not fix an inflation problem, it just removes the Fed's room to maneuver.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story, a violent repricing in storage. Seagate fell 10.2% on Friday to $848.99, and Western Digital dropped more than 10% to close at $415.29, with a 16% drop intraday. The trigger was a Nikkei report that Toshiba will spend roughly 60 billion yen to double its hard-disk output. Sandisk and Micron slid too, though sources disagree on the size of those moves.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Think about what that is. The scarcity premium in AI storage was repriced in a single session by the prospect of one competitor adding capacity, on the same day Nvidia pushed the Nasdaq to an intraday record. It says the market is now pricing the AI trade as a series of bottlenecks, and any bottleneck that looks like it will clear gets punished immediately.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In India, Bajaj Finance's board approved a raise of up to 17,500 crore rupees on October 1st. That is a 11,700 crore qualified institutional placement plus 5,800 crore of warrants issued to the promoter, Bajaj Finserv, with at least 25% paid upfront and the rest on exercise. The structure keeps the promoter stake at 51.30%. It needs shareholder approval at an EGM, and the shares rose 4% to 5% today on the raise and a solid quarterly business update.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The warrants are the signal. The promoter is committing its own capital alongside a dilutive QIP, which investors read as confidence, and it lets the lender grow its book without the stake dropping below the control line.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Over in Latin America and Europe, Bloomberg reports that Eni and Repsol are weighing a sale of part of Venezuela's Perla gas field. Each company owns 50% of the Cardón IV offshore block, which produces about 580 million cubic feet a day, all of it consumed domestically, with a target of about 1,200. They have signed with Caracas to begin exporting gas by the end of 2031.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Selling down is how they fund that expansion without overexposing their balance sheets, while Washington pushes to unlock Venezuelan energy. The export date, 2031, is a reminder that gas projects there are a long-duration bet on political stability.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The full Friday close is on the Markets tab, so let's spend this segment on the argument. One move was big enough to name: Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 2.6% on its first session after the holiday, its steepest drop since March, led by banks and tech.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And that is a Golden Week story as much as a markets story. Mainland exchanges were shut, so Hong Kong had to absorb a week of news by itself, and the tape was telling you that the consumption story in China is not as strong as the travel numbers suggest. We will come back to that in the China segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Everywhere else, the tape was friendly on the surface: US stocks rose after the jobs miss, the Nasdaq touched a record, and Europe was higher. But the S&P and the Dow still finished the week lower.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: My opinion is that the market is carrying 2 incompatible stories at once. The first is that the labor market is cracking, which argues for lower rates. The second is that a 10-year yield around 5.28%, not far from a more than 2-decade high, is the price of an inflation shock the Fed cannot ignore. Gold is the cleanest expression of that tension: it fell about 3.3% on the week, its 5th weekly loss in 6, because high real yields and a strong dollar beat every safe-haven bid.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What to watch this week is Wednesday's Fed minutes, and next week's inflation data. If the minutes show a hike was seriously discussed, the jobs miss becomes less of a rescue and more of a trap.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One more detail for the oil watchers. West Texas settled at about $91 a barrel, down 1.9% on Friday, as the G7 and IEA reserve release took the edge off prices. Brent is still above $102, so the market is not calling an all-clear.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Our deep dive today is a long way from tariffs and capex. It comes from The Economist, which this weekend ran a leader headlined, roughly, that mirror life is dangerous and regulators must act before it becomes real, plus an explainer saying it may soon be possible to create it. We should be clear that the full articles are paywalled and we are working from the headlines and the open reporting around them, so what follows is the public record, not a reading of the piece itself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Start with the chemistry, because it is elegant. Many of the molecules of life come in 2 mirror-image forms, like left and right hands. Our proteins are built from left-handed amino acids, and our DNA and RNA use right-handed sugars. Mirror life would be an organism built from the opposite hands: a bacterium with mirror-image proteins, mirror-image DNA, a complete reflection of biology.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And why would anyone want one? Researchers can already synthesize mirror-image DNA and proteins, and those molecules have appeal. Mirror proteins could make drugs that the body does not degrade. The leap from there to a full mirror cell is the one that worries people.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The alarm bell was a paper in Science in December 2024, a policy forum piece called Confronting risks of mirror life. It had 38 authors, accompanied by a 299-page technical report, and notably some of the authors had themselves worked toward this goal before changing their minds. Their core argument is about immunity. Our immune systems, and the viruses and predators that keep bacterial populations in check, rely on chiral recognition, on molecules fitting together like a glove. A mirror bacterium could slip past all of that.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The report called it plausible, even likely, that a sufficiently robust mirror bacterium could spread as an opportunistic pathogen across humans, animals and plants, with no natural enemy to control it. That is not a lab-containment problem in the usual sense, because the usual containment logic assumes the organism's biology is something the world already knows how to fight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Now the timeline, which is what makes this a governance story. Estimates range from about 10 to 30 years, so the capability does not exist. That is rare. Usually regulators arrive after the technology does, which is the story of social media and, arguably, of AI. Here a group of scientists is trying to draw a red line before the field has crossed it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And they have moved quickly. In February 2025 a gathering in the spirit of the Asilomar conference produced an entreaty signed by nearly 100 experts: mirror life should not be created unless future work shows it would not pose severe risks. By April 2025 that grew to 96 experts from more than 20 countries backing a moratorium, followed by meetings at the Institut Pasteur in Paris, then in Manchester, with further sessions in California and Japan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The money side matters. The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation and Renaissance Philanthropy both said they will not fund work aimed at creating a mirror organism, which is the cheapest and fastest form of regulation, because most of science runs on grants. UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee recommended a precautionary global moratorium. And in March 2026 the UN Secretary-General's Scientific Advisory Board published a brief calling for red lines, safety and monitoring practices, and policy well before feasibility.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So here is the uncomfortable fact. With all of that, there is still no binding national regulation anywhere. It is a norm and a funding boycott, not a law. The Congressional Research Service has an explainer on biosafety oversight, which tells you the US is still working out which agency would even own this.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The real dispute is about scope. Hardliners want to restrict even early-stage work on mirror components, because capability accumulates quietly. Others argue that mirror proteins and other building blocks are valuable for medicine and that over-restriction kills legitimate research. MIT Technology Review put it bluntly in April under the headline that no one is sure whether synthetic mirror life will kill us all, while the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists in August called it a mass-extinction risk we do not need to take.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There is also a caveat I like for balance: a computational preprint last December found reduced antibiotic binding to mirror bacterial targets, which would make mirror infections harder to treat. We have not read it, so treat it as a flag, not a conclusion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Why does this belong on a show for people who work in infrastructure and capital allocation? Because it is a clean test of precautionary governance. The pattern in your world is that the build comes first and the rules come after the first big failure: interconnection queues, data-center siting, grid reliability. Mirror life is the opposite case, a field choosing to be restrained by consensus before the first mistake.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the skeptic's reading is that consensus without enforcement is fragile. A single well-funded lab in a jurisdiction that never signed anything could change that, which is why the push is now for formal national rules and an international framework, not just voluntary pledges. We will keep an eye on whether any government actually puts it in law.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Energy today runs on the same theme as the market: schedules slipping and who pays. First, PJM. FERC accepted most of PJM's one-time Reliability Backstop Procurement on September 29th, but suspended it until February 28th, 2027. PJM had planned to take offers from September 30th through October 21st, and that window is now pulled. The Utility Dive weekender headline was that the FERC chair slams the PJM mess.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What were the concerns?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Cost allocation, rules for transmission owners that want to exit, and collateral requirements on load-serving entities. FERC wants large loads, meaning data centers, to be the ones paying. Commissioner Rosner's concurrence floated assigning costs to the specific zones where data-center growth is happening. For a developer, the five-month slip is the practical news: any project counting on backstop procurement for capacity value now has to carry that schedule risk into 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second, nuclear. Amazon and Constellation announced a 20-year power purchase agreement at Calvert Cliffs in Maryland on September 30th, covering 690 megawatts, including a roughly 190-megawatt uprate that comes online between 2030 and 2032. It funds more than $3 billion of upgrades across the 1,790-megawatt plant, and a related retail supply agreement covers Amazon's operations in PJM.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The twist is that there is no data center at the site, and the power still flows into the PJM grid. Amazon filed a conceptual plan in May for data-center campuses of 2.4 million square feet at Calvert Cliffs and withdrew it in August after voter backlash in Calvert County's June primary. So the hyperscaler got the electrons and dropped the building. The price was not disclosed, so we will not guess one. It also gives Constellation revenue certainty while it seeks a 20-year license extension.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third, the utility plan with the biggest numbers. Ameren Missouri filed a 20-year integrated resource plan on September 28th with 10.6 gigawatts of new gas. Gas goes from about 5% of the mix to about 60% by 2045, with coal going to zero.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The gas breakdown is specific: 2,100 megawatts of combined-cycle by 2031, 2,800 by 2035 and 1,400 by 2042, plus simple-cycle of 1,900 megawatts by 2029 and 2,400 after 2040, and 500 megawatts of gas fuel cells by 2030. Alongside it are 3.6 gigawatts of solar, 1.5 of wind, 2.4 of storage and 1.2 of nuclear. The line to underline is large load: Ameren now commits to serve 2.8 gigawatts of large load by 2030, versus 1.5 gigawatts assumed in its 2025 plan, and expects base deliveries to grow 60% between 2027 and 2030.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A trade site cites a $31.8 billion capital figure, but that is secondary sourcing so I would hold it loosely.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fourth, the question of who pays for keeping old plants alive. FERC rejected TransAlta's cost-recovery plan for the Centralia coal unit in Washington on October 1st. TransAlta wanted $19.9 million from the first 90-day Department of Energy order, issued in mid-December, which blocked the unit's planned retirement. FERC said the spread was too broad, since it included CAISO and SPP, and that any refiling must be limited to the Northwest assessment area. It also said the not-a-capacity-resource language in the orders does not bar compensation for costs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the practical lesson is that the cost of a keep-alive order is being treated as a regional cost-allocation question, and not a national one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fifth, Congress. A bipartisan Senate bill, the American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, was introduced October 1st, with Heinrich, Lee and Capito named in coverage. It would give FERC permitting authority over transmission lines above 230 kilovolts when in the public interest, without a prior DOE corridor designation, eliminate those national interest corridors, and bar incumbents from a federal right of first refusal on lines selected in regional or interregional plans. It is a bill, not law, but the right-of-first-refusal piece is the one that reshapes who builds transmission.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And last, an industry counter-move. Bloomberg reports a Lone Star Infrastructure Coalition in Texas, with Blackstone's QTS, NextEra, Siemens Energy, Quanta, the Nuclear Energy Institute and Lancium, led by Jimmy Glotfelty, a former Texas PUC commissioner and DOE official. It will engage mayors and county officials directly. The context cited is that about 120 data-center projects worth nearly $200 billion were blocked nationwide in the first half of 2026.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Calvert Cliffs story and this one are the same story. Local opposition is now a gating item as real as turbines and transformers, and the industry is finally organizing around it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Magandang umaga sa lahat. Ngayong araw, dalawang salita ang pag-aaralan natin, at pareho itong makikita sa balita mula sa Pilipinas. Ang una ay "hinarang."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Tama. Ang "hinarang" ay galing sa salitang "harang." Ibig sabihin, may humadlang sa daraanan mo, kaya hindi ka makausad. Madalas itong gamitin sa balita kapag may sasakyan, barko, o tao na pinigilan sa kanilang daan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At may kaibahan ito sa "hinadlangan." Ang "hinadlangan" ay mas malawak ang kahulugan, puwedeng plano, proyekto, o pangarap ang hinadlangan. Ang "hinarang" naman ay mas pisikal, parang may aktuwal na pader o barko sa harap mo.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa: "Hinarang ng mga barko ng China Coast Guard ang pangkat ng Philippine Coast Guard malapit sa Pag-asa." Pansinin, walang sinasabing opinyon dito. Simpleng paglalarawan ito ng nangyari, kaya paborito ito ng mga reporter.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay "pagkaantala." Galing ito sa "antala," at tumutukoy ito sa pagkahuli o pagkabalam ng isang bagay. Ito ang kalagayan ng pagiging naantala.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Madalas itong ipagkamali sa "ipagpaliban." Pero magkaiba sila. Ang "ipagpaliban" ay sadyang pagpapaliban, may nagpasya na ilipat ang petsa. Ang "pagkaantala" ay ang mismong pagkahuli, at kadalasan ay hindi sinasadya.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Halimbawa: "Ang pagkaantala ng testimonya ng AMLC ay nagbigay ng dagdag na oras sa depensa." Puwede rin itong gamitin sa biyahe, sa proyekto, o sa paghahatid ng serbisyo, kaya napaka-kapaki-pakinabang na salita.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sa pangkaraniwang usapan, mas madalas mong maririnig ang "delay," pero sa balita at sa pormal na sulatin, "pagkaantala" ang gamit. Subukan ninyong gamitin ang dalawang salitang ito ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sa Pilipinas, nagsimula ang linggo sa tensiyon sa karagatan. Noong Linggo, hinarang ng mga barko ng China Coast Guard ang pangkat ng Philippine Coast Guard na humahabol sa isang bangkang pinaghihinalaang gumagamit ng pampasabog sa pangingisda malapit sa Pag-asa Island.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sa Senado naman, may bagong pagkaantala sa paglilitis kay Bise Presidente Sara Duterte. Ipinagpaliban ni Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero ang testimonya ng direktor ng AMLC upang bigyan ng oras ang depensa na pag-aralan ang mga rekord. Sabi ng mga ulat, ibababa ng mga taga-usig ng Kamara ang paratang na panunuhol at itutuon ang pansin sa ebidensiyang sa tingin nila ay makakapagpatunay ng kasalanan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Let's add the detail in English. The incident was near Sandy Cays 2 and 3, about 3 nautical miles west of Pag-asa. Chinese Coast Guard vessel 21581 came within about 10 yards of a PCG boat, and a PLA Navy helicopter circled the team 4 times, which the PCG called an unnecessary act of intimidation. The team reached the suspect boat around 10 a.m. and ordered it to stop, but it ran southwest toward Zamora Reef and the Filipino team broke off for safety.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the trial, this is day 33 of the proceedings, focused on unexplained wealth. The AMLC testimony covers suspicious and covered transaction summaries involving 15 juridical persons from 2007 to 2025. Rappler framed the delay partly around confidentiality rules. The trial began July 6th.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The economy is the bigger pressure point this week. The Philippine Statistics Authority releases September inflation on Tuesday. A BusinessWorld poll expects a 4-month high, and Philstar's poll puts the figure at 6.7%, which would be the fastest in about 3.5 years. The drivers are habagat flooding that lifted food prices, rice, a weak peso and fuel.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the growth picture got worse this morning. AMRO's ASEAN+3 outlook cut the Philippines' 2026 GDP forecast to 3.3% from 4.1% in July, and 2027 to 4.6% from 5.5%, citing inflation hurting consumption and subdued public investment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The peso is hovering near 63 per dollar, and MUFG expects one more BSP hike in October, with the central bank more hawkish than the Fed. That is the same shape as our whole show today: a growth slowdown and an inflation problem at the same time, and a central bank with no easy move.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both tied to the China story coming up. The first is a structure: 宁可…也不…, meaning would rather do one thing than another.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The key idea is that you accept a real cost to avoid something worse. It is neutral to slightly written in register, and it sets up a preference with a price attached. Example: 消费者宁可存钱，也不愿多花钱。 (Consumers would rather save than spend more.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Compare it with 与其…不如, which you may already know. With 与其, you are criticizing option A and recommending option B, as in 与其抱怨，不如行动。 (Rather than complain, you might as well act.) 宁可 is different, because both options are bad and you pick the lesser evil. 宁可亏钱，也不冒险。 (I would rather lose money than take the risk.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A useful pattern: after 也不, the verb is usually something like 愿意, 肯 or 想, so you see 也不愿, 也不肯. That is how you spot it in finance writing about cautious buyers and cautious lenders.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second word is 反映出, to reflect or to reveal. It is an abstract collocation, and it lives in the written, news register.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Typical objects are abstractions: 反映出问题 (reveals a problem), 反映出信心 (reflects confidence), 反映出趋势 (reflects a trend). Example: 人均花费下降反映出消费者的谨慎。 (The drop in per-person spending reflects consumer caution.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The near-synonym to contrast is 表明. 表明 is firmer, it means demonstrates, as in 数据表明经济正在恢复。 (The data demonstrate that the economy is recovering.) 反映 is softer, more like mirrors, a signal that can be read different ways. Analysts use 反映出 when they want to hedge.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So if you are writing about a weak number, 反映出 is the cautious choice and 表明 is the confident one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管国庆假期出行人次不断增加，但是人均花费反映出消费者仍然很谨慎。 (Although the number of holiday trips keeps rising, per-person spending reflects that consumers are still very cautious.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is the two-speed picture in one sentence. Start with the factory and services side. Private PMIs for September came in strong: manufacturing at 52.1 from 51.5, services at 51.6 from 51.4, with services new business at its fastest since June.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: But the household side looks different. Reports said per-trip spending during the holiday was about 911 yuan, down 0.55% from a year earlier and the lowest since 2022. We could not confirm whether that figure was a pre-holiday forecast or the final tally, so treat it as indicative. Trip.com said bookings for 7 nights or more were up 123% and multi-destination itineraries up 84%, so volume rises while ticket size falls.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 消费者宁可多走几个地方，也不愿多花钱。 (Consumers would rather visit more places than spend more money.) That is a stylized version, but it matches the data.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The backdrop is the debt-deflation lens: second-quarter growth of 4.3% year on year, down from 5.0% in the first, deflation in its 10th straight quarter, and new-home prices in the big cities 15% to 30% below peak. Strong factories and cautious households is exactly why Hong Kong sold off 2.6% on Friday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start with the best art-market story of the week. A painting by Gertrude Abercrombie, the Chicago surrealist known as the queen of the bohemian artists, was bought at a Michigan estate sale for $30, reportedly at something like a flea-market price, and sold on October 1st at Freeman's in New York for a record $1.3 million, according to The Art Newspaper.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It matters beyond the anecdote. Abercrombie painted quiet, strange interiors, women and owls and moonlit rooms, with a deadpan stillness that sits between Magritte and Edward Hopper, and for decades she was treated as a regional figure. A record at a regional-minded sale suggests the re-evaluation of women surrealists is working its way down from the blue-chip evening sales to the estate market.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At the top of the market, Sotheby's will offer Van Gogh's Blossoming Chestnut Trees on November 18th, with an estimate of about $180 million on the hammer, around $207 million with the buyer's premium, and it is billed as a record-price Van Gogh. The Art Newspaper's broader point is that the auction houses' 2026 recovery has been carried by single-owner collection sales, and that the trickle-down to the rest of the market has been slower.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A late-season Van Gogh with those chestnut blossoms is a painting of exuberance from a man in the last 2 years of his life, which makes the estimate feel like it prices in the myth as much as the picture. Still, one lot at this level will tell us whether the second half's liquidity is real.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In music, the Gramophone Classical Music Awards are on Wednesday, October 7th, at the Grand Connaught Rooms in London, with the shortlist out and winners revealed at the ceremony. OperaWire also reviewed the world premiere of Michel van der Aa's new opera, The Theory of Flames, at the Opera Forward Festival in Amsterdam. We have not seen the production, so we will simply flag it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And a teaser for Thursday: the Nobel Prize in Literature is announced October 8th at 1 p.m. Central European time. The bookmakers have their lists, and as usual the safest prediction is that the winner will be someone half the audience has not read.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Our op-ed this morning is from Sherry Turkle in The Washington Post, published Sunday, headlined, roughly, AI can resurrect the dead, ask my chatbot mom. It is adapted from her book Artificial Intimacy, and the subtitle calls grief tech playing with fire.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Her experiment was striking. Turkle asked ChatGPT to role-play her mother, who died in 1968, feeding it her own 2021 memoir as the source. She found it seductive and disturbing at the same time. The steelman is this: a griever gets a chance to rehearse the unfinished conversation, but the avatar is built entirely from your own projections, so it lets you skip the work of mourning and weakens your grip on what is real.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There is a real argument there. Grief is the process of accepting that someone is gone, and a machine that answers back is designed to prevent exactly that acceptance.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Now the counter-take. People have always talked to the dead: letters, graveside conversations, prayer, the empty chair in therapy. A chatbot is a new medium for an old human habit, and for some mourners it may help, so declaring it playing with fire can sound paternalistic. And there is a fair question about the framing, because a book-promotion op-ed is always an argument for the book's thesis. Also, one anecdote with her own memoir as the training text is a thin base for a broad claim.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: My view is that the piece is strongest where it is least general, because the most useful finding is her own discomfort. If the person who has spent 4 decades studying our relationships with machines found it disturbing, that is worth more than a policy proposal.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A shorter second item, an editorial from the Washington Post's board titled, roughly, More government won't fix Britain. The argument is that 6 prime ministers in 10 years each promised more spending, and Andy Burnham would be the 7th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter-take is that the austerity years are what broke the services in the first place, so asking for less state after that is a convenient place to start the clock.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Our good thing this morning is a man named Jon Avery, who works as a valet at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Every patient who pulls up gets a smile, a Buffalo Bills hat, and the same 3 words: you got this. He says his aim is a meaningful encounter that is not hollow, and for people arriving for treatment, he is the first face they see that day.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One of those patients, Kate Fink, survived, and she and her colleagues at West Herr Automotive Group raised money to thank him. They got him Bills tickets and field passes.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That is the kind of story that needs no editorializing. A valet's job is to park a car, and he decided it was something more. Thank you for spending your morning with us. I'm Alex.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And I'm Sam. We will see you tomorrow on The Morning Commute.
